events.text:
**Britannica (1771–1797, "Damps" entry, row 1214, page 638)** describes inflammable air in coal mines as a gas that explodes with the force of gunpowder when ignited by miners' candles; it follows Dr. Priestley's chemistry (air generated underground from coal/phlogiston, water, and earth's heat, collecting where ventilation doesn't reach); and it prescribes burning it off by sending a man flat on the ground with a candle on a pole, since the inflammable air is lighter than other air and rises — or, where it has accumulated too much, ventilating the mine through perpendicular openings to create a draft.

**Wikipedia (Firedamp, page 505455, revision 1345728236)** defines firedamp as "any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane," found especially where the coal is bituminous, accumulating in pockets in coal and adjacent strata and exploding when released; "damp" is the collective name for mine gases, alongside blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp, and afterdamp.

**Evidence**

- Britannica `[B:1214:0]` — raw 18th-century OCR (long s read as `f`, broken words, e.g. "infammake", "Priefley", "wason", "explofion"):
  - "...the force exerted by it ... equal to that of gun powder."
  - "Dr Priefley has flown [shown], that inflammable air is comprised of pure elementary fire charcoal or phologines and stable veter [fixed air]; and that this composition may take place even in wason [water]."
  - Coal "...is abundantly able to supply the phogililon [phlogiston]... may be sufficient to produce a quantity of fullammable [inflammable] air, which gradually ... in chois [chosen?] places where it is not ... atmospheric air to carry it off..."
  - Prevention: "letting fire to it"; "...the insanhammable air, being much lighter than any other kind will naturally fit [rise] to the day [top] so that a man, lying flat on the ground to avoid the force of the explofion [explosion], and holding up a lighted candle fixed upon a pole, you at once fee [free] the mine from ... a troublehome [troublesome] good [guest?]."
  - Alternative: "produce a confluent [constant?] circulation of air as much as possible through all parts of the mine" via "a perpendicular opening, which they call haunk or flaqls [shaft?]".

- Wikipedia `[W:505455:1345728236]`:
  - "Firedamp is any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane. It is particularly found in areas where the coal is bituminous. The gas accumulates in pockets in the coal and adjacent strata and, when they are penetrated, the release of the gas can cause explosions."
  - "Damp is the collective name given to all gases (other than air) found in coal mines..." with blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp (hydrogen sulfide), and afterdamp (carbon monoxide) listed.

**Caveats**

- The linkage is an **uncertain match**: the Britannica entry's best Wikipedia candidate is `Firedamp` but the pair status is `no_clear_counterpart` (rerank logit -4.46, margin 0.48), and no saved comparison exists, so this is not a verified pair.
- The Britannica text is raw OCR with errors; I quote it raw and decoded where legible. The scan at page 638 confirms the general sense but I could not verify every garbled word.

**Inference** (not a cited fact): Both sides agree that inflammable gas in coal mines explodes when ignited and that airflow/ventilation is the key control; Britannica's phlogiston-based generation theory and candle-burning practice are obsolete, while Wikipedia identifies the gas as methane (coalbed methane).

**Britannica (1771–1797, "Damps" entry, row 1214, page 638)** describes inflammable air in coal mines as a gas that explodes with the force of gunpowder when ignited by miners' candles; it follows Dr. Priestley's chemistry (air generated underground from coal/phlogiston, water, and earth's heat, collecting where ventilation doesn't reach); and it prescribes burning it off by sending a man flat on the ground with a candle on a pole, since the inflammable air is lighter than other air and rises — or, where it has accumulated too much, ventilating the mine through perpendicular openings to create a draft.

**Wikipedia (Firedamp, page 505455, revision 1345728236)** defines firedamp as "any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane," found especially where the coal is bituminous, accumulating in pockets in coal and adjacent strata and exploding when released; "damp" is the collective name for mine gases, alongside blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp, and afterdamp.

**Evidence**

- Britannica `[B:1214:0]` — raw 18th-century OCR (long s read as `f`, broken words, e.g. "infammake", "Priefley", "wason", "explofion"):
  - "...the force exerted by it ... equal to that of gun powder."
  - "Dr Priefley has flown [shown], that inflammable air is comprised of pure elementary fire charcoal or phologines and stable veter [fixed air]; and that this composition may take place even in wason [water]."
  - Coal "...is abundantly able to supply the phogililon [phlogiston]... may be sufficient to produce a quantity of fullammable [inflammable] air, which gradually ... in chois [chosen?] places where it is not ... atmospheric air to carry it off..."
  - Prevention: "letting fire to it"; "...the insanhammable air, being much lighter than any other kind will naturally fit [rise] to the day [top] so that a man, lying flat on the ground to avoid the force of the explofion [explosion], and holding up a lighted candle fixed upon a pole, you at once fee [free] the mine from ... a troublehome [troublesome] good [guest?]."
  - Alternative: "produce a confluent [constant?] circulation of air as much as possible through all parts of the mine" via "a perpendicular opening, which they call haunk or flaqls [shaft?]".

- Wikipedia `[W:505455:1345728236]`:
  - "Firedamp is any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane. It is particularly found in areas where the coal is bituminous. The gas accumulates in pockets in the coal and adjacent strata and, when they are penetrated, the release of the gas can cause explosions."
  - "Damp is the collective name given to all gases (other than air) found in coal mines..." with blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp (hydrogen sulfide), and afterdamp (carbon monoxide) listed.

**Caveats**

- The linkage is an **uncertain match**: the Britannica entry's best Wikipedia candidate is `Firedamp` but the pair status is `no_clear_counterpart` (rerank logit -4.46, margin 0.48), and no saved comparison exists, so this is not a verified pair.
- The Britannica text is raw OCR with errors; I quote it raw and decoded where legible. The scan at page 638 confirms the general sense but I could not verify every garbled word.

**Inference** (not a cited fact): Both sides agree that inflammable gas in coal mines explodes when ignited and that airflow/ventilation is the key control; Britannica's phlogiston-based generation theory and candle-burning practice are obsolete, while Wikipedia identifies the gas as methane (coalbed methane).

results.title: Firedamp
results.passage:
Firedamp is any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane. It is particularly found in areas where the coal is bituminous. The gas accumulates in pockets in the coal and adjacent strata and, when they are penetrated, the release of the gas can cause explosions. Historically, if such a pocket was highly pressurized, it was termed a "bag of foulness".

Damp is the collective name given to all gases (other than air) found in coal mines in Great Britain and North America.

As well as firedamp, other damps include blackdamp (nonbreathable mixture of carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases); whitedamp (carbon monoxide and other gases produced by combustion); poisonous, explosive stinkdamp (hydrogen sulfide), with its characteristic rotten-egg odour; and the insidiously lethal afterdamp (carbon monoxide and other gases) which are produced following explosions of firedamp or coal dust.

results.title: Firedamp whistle
results.passage:
A firedamp whistle (German: Schlagwetterpfeife) is an instrument for the prophylactic indication of firedamp, flammable gases often present in coal mines.

The German Emperor Wilhelm II asked Fritz Haber in 1912, shortly after the opening of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physical Chemistry and Electrochemistry in Berlin, for the construction of a warning system for the presence of firedamp.

Within a year Haber had developed the firedamp whistle and presented it to the emperor in a lecture on 28 October 1913. Haber tried hard to market the device, and eventually signed a contract with the Auergesellschaft. The device did not prevail, since the calibration of the pipes under working conditions in a colliery was not practical.

results.title: Safety lamp
results.passage:
A safety lamp is any of several types of lamp that provides illumination in places such as coal mines where the air may carry coal dust or a build-up of flammable gases, which may explode if ignited, possibly by an electric spark. Until the development of effective electric lamps in the early 1900s, miners used flame lamps to provide illumination. Open flame lamps could ignite flammable gases which collected in mines, causing explosions; safety lamps were developed to enclose the flame to prevent it from igniting the explosive gases. Flame safety lamps have been replaced for lighting in mining with sealed explosion-proof electric lights, but continue to be used to detect gases.

Miners have traditionally referred to the various gases encountered during mining as damps, from the Middle Low German word dampf (meaning " vapour "). Damps are variable mixtures and are historic terms.

Firedamp – Naturally occurring flammable mixtures, principally methane.

Blackdamp or chokedamp – Nitrogen

results.title: Davy lamp
results.passage:
The Davy lamp is a safety lamp used in flammable atmospheres, invented in 1815 by Sir Humphry Davy. It consists of a wick lamp with the flame enclosed inside a mesh screen. It was created for use in coal mines, to reduce the danger of explosions due to the presence of methane and other flammable gases, called firedamp or minedamp.

German polymath Alexander von Humboldt, working for the German Bureau of Mines, had concerns for the health and welfare of the miners and invented a kind of respirator and "four lamps of different construction suitable for employment in various circumstances. The respirator was to prevent the inhaling of injurious gases, and to supply the miner with good air; the lamps were constructed to burn in the most inflammable kind of fire-damp without igniting the gas. They were the forerunners of Davy's later invention, and were frequently made use of by the miners."
